title: Love without pretending (Romans 12:9–21)
hook: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep; overcome evil with good

segments.voice: Yesterday, a living sacrifice, a whole ordinary day offered, and your line was be transformed. Did you swap one thing that squeezes you for one that renews? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Your friend texts: I got the job! And somewhere in your chest, just for a second, something tightens. You wanted that kind of news. You type back: so happy for you!!! with three exclamation points, and you mean it, mostly. Or someone you can't stand has a terrible week, and a small, ugly part of you feels something that isn't quite sympathy. Everybody has these moments. Love is easy to perform. The emojis are right there. Paul, having asked for a living sacrifice, now gets very practical. He fires off a list of short commands, almost like a text thread. And the first one is about pretending.
screen: `I GOT THE JOB!` → `SOMETHING TIGHTENS.` → `LOVE IS EASY TO PERFORM.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in the King James Bible: "Let love be without dissimulation." Dissimulation is an old word for pretending. The Greek is anupokritos: without hypocrisy. And a hypokrites, in Greek, was an actor, someone speaking from behind a stage mask. So Paul is saying: let love take off the mask. Then comes the rapid list. Hate what is evil, hold on to what is good. Outdo one another in showing honor. Be patient in trouble. Keep praying. Share with those in need. Welcome strangers. And then two lines that are harder than they sound: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." The weeping is often the easier one. It's rejoicing with someone whose good news stings that takes real love, the kind with no mask. Then Paul goes further, into enemies. Bless those who persecute you. Don't pay back evil for evil. If it be possible, he says, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. As much as depends on you, because sometimes it doesn't. Leave vengeance to God. And then, quoting Proverbs: "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Coals of fire sounds like revenge, but most readers hear it as the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you've wronged, the kind that might change a heart. Nobody's completely sure where the image comes from. And the last line of the chapter sums it all up: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." You can hear Jesus's own teaching behind it: love your enemies, bless those who curse you.
screen: `A HYPOCRITE WAS AN ACTOR IN A MASK.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM THAT DO REJOICE.` · `AS MUCH AS LIETH IN YOU.` · `FEED YOUR ENEMY: COALS OF FIRE.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL WITH GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice with someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has good news right now. A promotion, a baby, a trip, a new love, a win. If there's a little tightness when you think of them, notice it honestly; that's all right. Then picture their face when they got the news. Let yourself be glad with them, really glad, not performing. Breathe in their good news like it's partly yours. If you pray, you can thank God for their joy, by name. The bell holds the time.
Love without pretending. Anupokritos in Greek: love without the actor's mask, glad with the glad and sad with the sad.

Your line: overcome evil with good. Today, tell the person you thought of how glad you are for them, in your own words, no mask. And if someone wrongs you, answer with one good thing. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Romans 12:9–21 is often read at weddings and taught as a picture of everyday Christian love; many Christians try to live out "overcome evil with good" by answering wrongs with kindness.

original.note: Greek: without hypocrisy, unmasked. from hypokritēs, a stage actor.

trapdoor: what you thought: love without pretending means always being nice.
what it means: love with the mask off: glad at another's good news, sad at their grief, and answering evil with good.
what a scholar hears: anupokritos, un-acted, and the coals of fire come from Proverbs 25:21–22; one theory links them to an Egyptian ritual of repentance, but the origin is uncertain.

notes: Romans 12:18 is said in the voice ('if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men') without quotation marks; KJV wording believed exact. Keeper may want it formally cited as a quotation.
Coals of fire: the Egyptian penitential ritual theory (S. Morenz) is mentioned only as 'one theory' in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Hypokritēs as stage actor: standard. Confirm.
Link to Jesus's teaching (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27–28) is paraphrased.
